summary:
Astrion (formerly Project 101) is a space-science learning game that runs in your browser, built with React, TypeScript, Three.js and Phaser. You can fly around an interactive 3D Solar System, open illustrated study pages for all eight planets, and use the Planetary Characteristics toolkit to compare gravity, day length, years, temperature, moons and scale. Every lesson feeds into Outpost Command, an eight-mission campaign where you run a Mars outpost: sizing a Mercury solar rig, packing a Venus cargo flight, planning life support, picking a Mars site, shielding your crew from solar storms, plotting routes through the outer system, keeping everyone healthy on long missions, and making the big command call. Mass, power, heat, radiation and light-time delay push back at every choice, so you're weighing trade-offs instead of answering quiz questions. NASA fact-sheet values, DONKI space-weather events, EPIC imagery, mission photos and JPL distances keep it grounded, while simplified models keep it fun to play and are clearly labelled. Astrion tackles a problem: planetary science and engineering can feel abstract, so learners get to try things, make mistakes and see what happens, with no exams, locked levels or pressure. That matters because it builds data literacy, systems thinking and real curiosity about deep-space exploration, the skills and spark tomorrow's space explorers will need to take on the hardest problems on Earth and beyond.

details:
What it does and how it works

Astrion is a browser-based Junior Astronaut Trainer. It has two connected parts:

  • An interactive Solar System with study pages for all eight planets.
  • Outpost Command, a campaign where you build and run a Mars outpost while completing one engineering mission per planet.

Each mission turns a planetary fact into a design decision: Mercury’s intense sunlight affects solar power and cooling, Venus’s gravity affects cargo, Earth’s closed loops affect life support, Mars’s sites affect construction and radiation, Jupiter’s storms affect shielding, Saturn’s distance affects power and travel, Uranus’s distance creates light time delay, and Neptune tests command trade offs. Resources, crew health, supplies, and completed upgrades carry between missions. Results are recorded, and completingall eight produces a final debrief and certification.

The game saves locally in the browser. There is no account, backend, or personal-data collection.

Benefits

  • Turns reading into active decisions with immediate visual and numerical feedback.
  • Makes abstract ideas concrete: inverse square sunlight, launch mass, thermal 
  • limits, radiation dose, light-time delay, and closed-loop life support.
  • Encourages systems thinking: every improvement has a mass, power, or crew cost.
  • Works without accounts, installations, or a live NASA connection.
  • Supports classroom use through short missions, clear pass criteria, and a reset option.
  • Keeps accessibility in mind with keyboard focusable controls, click alternatives to 
  • drag, reduced-motion handling, and readable status labels.

Intended impact

The intended impact is to make planetary science and space engineering feel like something students can operate, not just memorise. Astrion is designed to build confidence with STEM ideas, show how scientific constraints shape real missions, and leave playerswith a better mental model of the Solar System and the engineering trade-offs involved in exploring it.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei.
  • Game layer: Phaser 4.2 for the outpost scene.
  • Tooling: Node.js/npm, TypeScript compiler, Oxlint, browser-based testing.
  • Hardware: A standard laptop or desktop with a modern browser. No special sensors, VR, or external hardware are required.

How the project is creative

Astrion treats the Solar System itself as the interface. Planet orbs, orbital visuals,  mission specific SVG instruments, and a Mars outpost map create a consistent visual  world instead of a sequence of worksheets. The newest controls make the engineering  feel tactile: players drag cargo onto a pallet, tap solar and cooling slots, load shield  materials, choose a power package, and drag commander’s orders into limited slots.  The mission briefings tie each interaction back to a real planetary science idea, and the  campaign turns eight separate topics into one continuing story.

Factors considered

  • Scientific accuracy vs playability: values are simplified but tied to documented  planetary characteristics and clearly labelled as illustrative.
  • Age appropriateness: no graphic content, no personal data, and consequences explained through science rather than punishment.
  • Accessibility: every drag action has a click fallback; controls use buttons, labels,  focus states, and reduced-motion handling.
  • Privacy: nickname only, saved locally; no accounts or analytics.
  • Classroom constraints: works offline after loading, runs in a browser, and can be  reset.
  • Performance: lightweight SVG/CSS mission models alongside the 3D scene, with  mobile layout fallbacks.
  • Assessment clarity: every live model now reports the same pass result used by the mission evaluator, so the status cannot disagree with the final verdict.
  • Scope and reliability: all eight mission paths were played through, not just built.
